lead: One chip, two transistors. CMOS gives high input impedance, low static power and dense logic. A bipolar transistor gives large transconductance and current drive. BiCMOS adds one vertical NPN to the CMOS flow with three or four extra masks, some before the wells and some after the gates. One die senses with CMOS and drives with bipolar. Uses: radio front ends, high-speed links, mixed-signal chips and power ICs.
prereq: You need the chapter on nMOS and CMOS fabrication process flow for the mask sequence, the chapter on p-well, n-well and twin-tub processes for wells, the chapter on oxidation, diffusion and ion implantation for doping, and MOSFET I-V characteristics and device equations for MOSFET transconductance.

blocks.text: An NPN has an n+ emitter, a p base and an n collector. In normal operation the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction is reverse biased, so electrons cross the thin base into the collector. Current gain is β = I<sub>C</sub> / I<sub>B</sub>, where I<sub>C</sub> is collector current and I<sub>B</sub> is base current. In an IC, β is typically 50 to 200.

The device is built vertically: a small n+ emitter window at the surface, a thin p base under it, and the n collector below. Current flows down into the wafer, so the device packs into a small area and the base can be very thin.

The collector must be lightly doped. It must hold the reverse bias of the base-collector junction without breaking down, and heavy doping would lower breakdown voltage and raise junction capacitance. Light doping means high resistivity, so the collector resistance R<sub>C</sub> is large: current travels a long, narrow n path to the collector contact, wasting voltage headroom and slowing the device.

Three steps fix this. A buried layer mask defines an n+ region in the p-substrate, implanted with arsenic or antimony at a heavy dose. A thin n-type epitaxial layer is grown over it and becomes the collector. A deep n+ sinker implant runs from the surface down to touch the buried layer, so collector current flows down a short, heavily doped pipe to the contact.

Epitaxial thickness is a trade-off. Thin epi gives low R<sub>C</sub>, so speed, but raises base-collector capacitance and lowers breakdown voltage. Thick, lightly doped epi holds high voltage and gives low capacitance, but R<sub>C</sub> is large. Neighbouring devices are separated by junction isolation: p-type regions surround each n island, so every pair of neighbours is held apart by a reverse-biased p-n junction.

sections.h3: Adding the NPN to the CMOS flow

blocks.text: The CMOS part is unchanged. Run the twin-tub flow (see p-well, n-well and twin-tub processes), but put the collector steps in front of it.

items: Start on a p-substrate. Grow pad oxide, expose the buried layer mask, implant n+ arsenic or antimony, strip the resist.
Grow thin, lightly doped n-type epitaxial silicon. This is the collector.
Sinker implant immediately after the epitaxy, before or with the n-well/p-well implants. The well drive-in also diffuses the sinker down to the buried layer.
Gate oxidation, poly deposition, gate mask and etch. Then n+ and p+ source/drain masks and the anneal.
Base mask: shallow p implant for the NPN base.
Emitter mask: shallow n+ arsenic implant for the emitter.

blocks.text: The order is fixed by the thermal budget. The buried layer goes first because the epitaxial growth and the well drive-in that follow are hot steps, and it must be diffused deep by them. The base is only a few tenths of a micrometre deep, so it comes after the hot steps, or is finished with a short low-temperature anneal. Extra heat spreads the base, and a wider base lowers both β and speed.

sections.h3: What it buys and what it costs

blocks.text: Transconductance is the payoff. For a bipolar transistor g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>T</sub>, where V<sub>T</sub> is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at room temperature. For a MOSFET in saturation g<sub>m</sub> = 2 I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>ov</sub>, where V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TH</sub> is the overdrive. At the same current the bipolar wins because V<sub>T</sub> is only 26 mV while a usable overdrive is a few hundred millivolts.
gm = IC / VT (bipolar) gm = 2 IC / Vov (MOSFET, saturation)

g<sub>m</sub> is transconductance in A/V; I<sub>C</sub> is collector or drain current in A; V<sub>T</sub> is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at 300 K; V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TH</sub> is the overdrive in V; V<sub>GS</sub> is gate-source voltage; V<sub>TH</sub> is MOSFET threshold voltage. V<sub>T</sub> and V<sub>TH</sub> are different quantities.

The second payoff is a nearly constant base-emitter voltage. V<sub>BE</sub> sits near 0.7 V over a wide current range, so a bipolar pair makes a stable reference, a current mirror and a sharp comparator. CMOS brings a gate that draws no DC input current, dense logic and near-zero static power, because it burns power only while switching.

The cost is process. BiCMOS needs three or four masks beyond CMOS: buried layer, sinker, base and emitter. Each adds lithography, etch and implant, so cycle time grows and yield falls, and every step after the base must stay cool. The extra n+ regions also join the parasitic p-n-p-n path, so latch-up care in layout matters more (see the chapter on latch-up in CMOS and its prevention).

Against pure bipolar, BiCMOS gives up a little speed for density and low power. Typical uses: radio front ends with an NPN low-noise amplifier, high-speed drivers and serial links, mixed-signal chips, and power ICs with a bipolar bandgap reference.

examples.question: An NPN in a BiCMOS process is biased at I<sub>C</sub> = 2 mA with β = 100, V<sub>T</sub> = 26 mV. (a) Find I<sub>B</sub> and g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>T</sub>. (b) An nMOS carries the same 2 mA with V<sub>ov</sub> = 0.5 V; find g<sub>m</sub> = 2 I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>ov</sub> and the ratio.
steps: I<sub>B</sub> = I<sub>C</sub> / β = 2 mA / 100 = 0.02 mA = 20 μA.
g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>T</sub> = 2 × 10⁻³ A / 26 × 10⁻³ V = 7.69 × 10⁻² A/V = 76.9 mA/V.
g<sub>m</sub> = 2 I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>ov</sub> = 4 mA / 0.5 V = 8 mA/V.
Ratio: 76.9 ÷ 8 = 9.6, so the bipolar has roughly ten times the transconductance at the same current.
examples.answer: I<sub>B</sub> = 20 μA, g<sub>m</sub>(NPN) = 76.9 mA/V, g<sub>m</sub>(MOS) = 8 mA/V; the bipolar has about 9.6 times the transconductance at 2 mA.

examples.question: At what overdrive V<sub>ov</sub> would the nMOS and the NPN have equal transconductance at equal current?
steps: Set I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>T</sub> = 2 I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>ov</sub>. The current cancels.

The square law would hand the MOSFET the larger g<sub>m</sub> below 52 mV, but there the MOSFET is close to weak inversion, where the square law fails and g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub>/(n·V<sub>T</sub>) with n about 1.3 to 1.5, still below the bipolar. Real overdrives are 200–500 mV, so the bipolar gives 4 to 10 times the transconductance.
examples.answer: The square law gives equal g<sub>m</sub> at V<sub>ov</sub> = 52 mV, and the ratio V<sub>ov</sub> / (2 V<sub>T</sub>) does not depend on current; in practice the bipolar has the larger g<sub>m</sub> at any equal current.

traps: Treating BiCMOS as plain CMOS plus one transistor. The buried layer, epitaxy and sinker are exactly what make the NPN fast, and what cost masks, yield and thermal budget.
Swapping buried layer and sinker. Both are n+; the buried layer is implanted before the epitaxy and lies under the device, the sinker is a deep implant from the surface down to it.
Assuming a higher β is always better. A thinner base raises β but lowers breakdown; lighter base doping raises β but raises base resistance. β is a design trade.
Getting the thermal order wrong. The buried layer goes first because epitaxy and well drive-in are hot; the shallow base goes late so it does not spread.

quiz.q: Define β for a bipolar transistor and give a typical IC value.
quiz.a: β = I<sub>C</sub> / I<sub>B</sub>, the ratio of collector current to base current in forward-active mode; typically 50 to 200 in an integrated NPN.

quiz.q: Why is an n+ buried layer placed under the collector?
quiz.a: It gives a low-resistance path from the collector contact to the active collector region, cutting the series resistance R<sub>C</sub> that wastes voltage headroom and slows the device.

quiz.q: Why is the NPN base formed after the well drive-in?
quiz.a: The base is only a few tenths of a micrometre deep. Well drive-in is a long, hot diffusion; a base present then would spread wider, lowering β and speed. So the base comes after, or with a short low-temperature anneal.

quiz.q: State the trade-off in choosing epitaxial collector thickness.
quiz.a: Thin epi lowers R<sub>C</sub> but raises base-collector capacitance and lowers breakdown voltage. Thick, lightly doped epi gives high breakdown and low capacitance at the cost of a large R<sub>C</sub>. Choose so the junction holds the supply with margin while R<sub>C</sub> stays small.

quiz.q: An NPN carries I<sub>C</sub> = 1 mA with β = 80 and V<sub>T</sub> = 26 mV. Find I<sub>B</sub> and g<sub>m</sub>.
quiz.a: I<sub>B</sub> = I<sub>C</sub> / β = 1 mA / 80 = 12.5 μA. g<sub>m</sub> = I<sub>C</sub> / V<sub>T</sub> = 1 mA / 26 mV = 38.5 mA/V.

quiz.q: Adding an NPN to a CMOS flow raises cost in three ways. Name them and link each to a process step.
quiz.a: Masks and steps: buried layer, sinker, base and emitter each add lithography, etch and implant, so cycle time grows. Area and yield: each NPN plus isolation takes more silicon than a CMOS gate, and more steps mean more defects, so yield falls. Thermal budget: the shallow base limits the temperature of every later step, so the emitter drive and the contact and metal anneals must be short and low-temperature.

beyond: Not for the exam. Adding germanium to the base makes a SiGe heterojunction bipolar transistor, which reaches cut-off frequencies of hundreds of GHz beside CMOS on one die; it is used in 5G, radar and optical-link chips. Search for SiGe HBT, fT and fmax, and BiCMOS RF front end.
